CPM, CPC, CPA, CPL, ROAS Explained: Which to Run On

Distribution

In short: CPM, CPC, CPL and CPA describe what a company pays for, and each hides what the next reveals. ROAS flatters. The number to manage the business on is customer acquisition cost against value over a realistic horizon, with payback period as the constraint.

Key points

  • CPM prices attention, not whether it was real; a low CPM often signals poor inventory.
  • A ROAS of four on a product with thirty percent gross margin is losing money.
  • CAC divides all acquisition spending, including fees, creative, tools and people, by new customers.
  • A channel with excellent LTV and an eighteen-month payback can still bankrupt a cash-limited company.
  • Run the week on the pricing metric closest to an observable outcome, and the quarter on CAC against horizon value.

Every media report is built on a small set of acronyms. They describe what was paid for and what came back, and each one hides something the others reveal.

The pricing acronyms: what you pay for

CPM, cost per mille (thousand impressions). The price of a thousand ad views. The oldest measure and the standard for programmatic and display. It tells you what attention costs, not whether the attention was real or did anything. A low CPM is often a symptom of poor inventory.

CPC, cost per click. What you pay each time someone clicks. The standard for search and much of social. Better than CPM because a click is an action, but clicks are cheap to generate and easy to fake, and a click is not a customer.

CPL, cost per lead. What you pay for a contact: a form, a sign-up, a download. The standard for business-to-business and any considered purchase. Useful only if "lead" is defined tightly; a loose definition produces cheap leads nobody can sell to.

CPA, cost per acquisition (or action). What you pay for a defined outcome: an account opened, a purchase made, a subscription started. The standard for performance marketing and affiliate programs. The closest of the pricing acronyms to something the finance team recognizes.

CPV, cost per view, for video and clipping programs, and CPI, cost per install, for apps, follow the same logic: a price for a defined event that may or may not lead to a customer.

The return acronyms: what you get back

ROAS, return on ad spend. Revenue attributed to advertising divided by the cost of the advertising. A ROAS of four means four dollars of attributed revenue for each dollar spent. Widely used, easy to calculate, and misleading in two ways: it depends entirely on how revenue was attributed, and it ignores every cost except media. A campaign with a ROAS of four on a product with thirty percent gross margin is losing money.

CAC, customer acquisition cost. All acquisition spending, media, fees, creative, tools, people, divided by the number of new customers. The honest cousin of CPA. Harder to compute, harder to game.

LTV, lifetime value, or more usefully, value over a defined horizon. What a customer is worth over twelve or twenty-four months, net of refunds, churn, and cost to serve. The number CAC has to be compared with for any of this to mean anything.

Payback period. How many months of a customer's contribution it takes to recover the cost of acquiring them. The measure a company with limited cash should watch most closely, because a channel with excellent LTV and an eighteen-month payback can still bankrupt it.

What each one hides

CPM hides whether the impression was real. CPC hides whether the click was interested. CPL hides whether the lead was qualified. CPA hides whether the acquired customer stayed. ROAS hides margin, non-media costs, and the attribution model. CAC hides nothing much, which is why fewer reports feature it.

Which one to run on

Run the week on the pricing acronym closest to the outcome you can observe: CPA where an outcome is trackable, CPL where the sale happens offline, CPC or CPM only where nothing further down the funnel can be measured yet.

Run the quarter on CAC against value over a realistic horizon, with payback as the constraint. And insist that every CPA, CPL, and ROAS figure in a report says which events the company's own tracking confirmed, rather than which events a partner or platform claimed.

A media partner who reports in CPM and ROAS but cannot produce CAC and payback is reporting what they were paid to deliver rather than what the company received.

lowob takeaway: CPM, CPC, CPL, and CPA describe what you pay for, each one hiding what the next reveals. ROAS flatters; CAC against horizon value, with payback as the constraint, is the number to manage the business on.

Common questions

What is the difference between CPA and CPL?

CPL is what you pay for a contact such as a form or sign-up, and is useful only if "lead" is defined tightly. CPA is what you pay for a defined outcome such as an account opened or purchase made.

Why is ROAS misleading?

It depends entirely on how revenue was attributed and ignores every cost except media. A campaign with a ROAS of four on a thirty percent gross margin product is losing money.

Which marketing metric should a company manage to?

Run the week on the pricing metric closest to the outcome you can observe, and the quarter on CAC against value over a realistic horizon, with payback period as the constraint.

What is payback period in marketing?

How many months of a customer's contribution it takes to recover the cost of acquiring them. It is the measure a company with limited cash should watch most closely.
